catalog_citation: LaPolla, Randy J. & Dory Poa. 2001. Rawang Texts, with Grammatical Analysis and English Translation. Berlin: LINCOM Europa. (Mvtwang dialect; open PDF on the author's site, held at the copy we hold)
catalog_locator: Introduction, section 'Transcription', printed p. vii = PDF page 8 (rendered page image read directly; scanned in the copy we, PAGE p-008)
catalog_quote: Tones are marked as follows (using the letter a as a base): high tone: á, mid tone: ā, low tone: à. All syllables that end in a stop consonant (-p, -t, -ʔ, -k) are in the high tone. Open syllables without a tone mark are unstressed. A colon marks non-basic long vowels. ... There are a number of morphophonemic processes which affect the segments and tones in connected speech. For example, when the negative mv- is added to a verb that has a vocalic prefix, the resulting form will combine the two, and it will become stressed and so given a tone, e.g. /mv-vpvt/ (NEG-give/put in) > [màpvt] "not put in". There are also often tone changes when certain suffixes, such as the reflexive/middle suffix -shì, is added to a verb.

The page reads, verbatim: 'Tones are marked as follows (using the letter a as a base): high tone: á, mid tone: ā, low tone: à. All syllables that end in a stop consonant (-p, -t, -ʔ, -k) are in the high tone. Open syllables without a tone mark are unstressed. A colon marks non-basic long vowels.' and further down: 'There are a number of morphophonemic processes which affect the segments and tones in connected speech. For example, when the negative mv- is added to a verb that has a vocalic prefix, the resulting form will combine the two,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Rawang is a register-tone language (high, mid, low on open/sonorant-final syllables; stop-final syllables are always high). Stress is not positional: every tone-bearing syllable is stressed, and the open syllables written without a tone mark — the schwa (v = [ə]) prefix syllables and particles — are unstressed and toneless. A prefix syllable that fuses with the negative mv- becomes stressed and thereby acquires a tone. In effect, in a prefix+root (sesquisyllabic) word the root syllable carries tone and stress and the prefix does not; the source does not state a syllable-count rule (e.g. 'final').
new_statements.exceptions: Morphophonemic fusion: prefix syllable fused with negative mv- becomes stressed and toned; tone changes with certain suffixes (e.g. reflexive/middle -shì). Morse 1988 (pp. 129-130) and Sarep 1996 (p. 104) independently describe the same two non-contrastive (neutral-tone) syllable classes — schwa CV prefix syllables and stop-final syllables — without using the word 'stress'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, stated as an orthographic/transcription convention for the Mvtwang (Mvt River) dialect, the standard written variety in Myanmar; connected-speech morphophonemics noted separately. The statement is brief (a transcription note, not a phonology chapter); the fuller primary phonology (Morse 1962, 1963) was not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted material describes the Mvtwang (Matwang/Metwang, 'Mvt River') dialect of Rawang, the written standard in Kachin State, Myanmar (Glottolog language rawa1265; no separate dialect code asserted). Sarep 1996 describes the Sinwal dialect (four tonemes, falling tone instead of low), Barnard 1934 the Wvdamkong dialect, and the LaPolla 2003/2017 sketch Glottolog lists under rawa1265 is Dulong (drun1238), a closely related variety on the Chinese side.

sources.note: Introduction, 'Transcription', p. vii: three tones (high á, mid ā, low à); stop-final syllables are high-toned; 'Open syllables without a tone mark are unstressed'; when negative mv- fuses with a vocalic prefix the fused syllable 'will become stressed and so given a tone' (/mv-vpvt/ > [màpvt]). Stress = tone-bearing; toneless open (schwa) prefix syllables are unstressed.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number Philol 950.55)
sources.note: No use of the word 'stress'. Tones pp. 128-130: register tone language with high [55], mid [33], low [11] on non-stop-final syllables plus a fourth 'neutral, non-contrastive tone' (Morse 1962:71); 'Rawang exhibits two classes of tonally non-contrastive syllables: a) prefixal open syllables of CV-pattern in which the V is [ə]. b) closed syllables of (C)VC pattern in which the final C is a stop' (p. 130). Apparent contour tones are two coalesced vowels across a morpheme boundary.

sources.note: Phonology sketch pp. 101-104: no stress statement. Syllable = nucleus + toneme; Sinwal has four tonemes: [55] high, [33] mid, [41] high-low falling (corresponds to Mvtwang low), and [00] 'neutral, non-contrastive tone' which 'occurs in syllables with a stop coda and in open syllables with the phoneme /ə/' (p. 104); neutral tone not.
